params.question: A 28-year-old with a malunited tibial fracture has normal-appearing AP and lateral radiographs, but clinically walks with a noticeable foot rotation abnormality. Which investigation is most appropriate to accurately quantify the rotational component of this malunion?

answers.text: Standing full-length radiograph on a long-leg cassette

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Standing X-rays assess mechanical axis alignment and angular deformity under load, but they cannot accurately measure rotational malunion — rotation requires cross-sectional imaging.

Plain X-rays cannot measure true rotational malunion accurately. A CT scanogram with 3D reconstruction defines the exact angle of twisting by comparing cross-sections at the fracture site with the bone ends.
Bone scanning assesses metabolic activity and viability of bone, not rotational alignment. It is reserved for cases where viability of the malunited segment is in question.

answers.text: Supine AP and lateral radiographs with joint views above and below

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Supine films underestimate functional angulation under load and still cannot quantify rotation. For lower-limb alignment, standing films are required — and even those do not measure rotation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Plain X-rays measure angulation and shortening well, but they cannot quantify rotational malunion. CT scanogram with 3D reconstruction is needed because it compares cross-sections at the fracture site with the bone ends to define the exact twist angle.
Exactly right. Rotational malunion is invisible on plain radiographs and requires CT scanogram with 3D reconstruction for accurate measurement.

interactions.label: A patient with a femoral shaft non-union shows abundant callus formation around

params.question: A patient with a femoral shaft non-union shows abundant callus formation around the fracture site on X-ray, but the fracture line remains clearly visible after nine months. What is the most appropriate primary treatment?

answers.text: Iliac crest autologous bone grafting with plate fixation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bone grafting addresses biological failure, which is the hallmark of atrophic non-union. Abundant callus here indicates intact biology — the problem is mechanical instability, not a biological deficit.
Staged debridement and bone transport is the protocol for infected non-union. There is no indication of infection in this scenario, and the abundant callus confirms active biological healing.

Abundant callus indicates hypertrophic non-union — biology is intact but mechanical stability is inadequate. IM nailing with reaming provides rigid fixation and stimulates endosteal vascularity and local growth factors, addressing the mechanical problem directly.

BMPs are biological adjuncts for atrophic non-union where the bone-forming stimulus has failed. They cannot substitute for mechanical stabilisation, which is the primary deficit in hypertrophic non-union.

overallFeedback.feedback: Abundant callus around the fracture site is the hallmark of hypertrophic non-union — biology is intact, but mechanical stability has failed. The treatment is rigid fixation alone (IM nailing with reaming for femur and tibia), not bone grafting or biological adjuncts.
Correct. Hypertrophic non-union has good biology (shown by abundant callus) but poor stability — rigid mechanical fixation alone, ideally by IM nailing with reaming, is the treatment.

interactions.label: The final Gustilo-Anderson grade of an open fracture should be assigned in the e

params.question: The final Gustilo-Anderson grade of an open fracture should be assigned in the emergency department based on the initial wound assessment.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: The final Gustilo-Anderson grade should only be assigned in the operating theatre, after thorough debridement, not in the emergency department. Wounds that look like Grade II on initial assessment often turn out to be Grade IIIA or IIIB once the true extent of soft tissue destruction becomes visible after dead tissue is removed.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. The final grade must only be assigned in the operating theatre after thorough debridement. Emergency department assessment frequently underestimates the true extent of soft tissue damage — wounds initially appearing Grade II often prove to be Grade IIIA or IIIB once devitalised tissue is removed.

params.question: An open tibial fracture classified as Gustilo-Anderson Grade III is brought to the emergency department. The orthopaedic team is preparing for surgical debridement. What is the most critical time-sensitive action for preventing secondary infection?

answers.text: Irrigate the wound thoroughly with antiseptic solution within 30 minutes

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Repeated wound irrigation in the ED disturbs healing tissue rather than helping it. The wound should be covered with a saline-moistened dressing, photographed once for documentation, and left undisturbed until the operating theatre.

answers.text: Begin surgical debridement within 6 hours of injury

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The 6-hour debridement rule is now considered obsolete. Current evidence shows that administering antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation is more important than debridement timing in preventing infection.

answers.text: Administer intravenous antibiotics within 1 hour of presentation

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Bacteria adhere to damaged tissue within minutes and form a protective biofilm within hours that shields them from both antibiotics and the immune system. Administering antibiotics within 1 hour reduces the bacterial load before this shield forms — the single most time-critical intervention for open fractures.

answers.text: Apply a pressure dressing and defer antibiotics until wound cultures are obtained

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Delaying antibiotics to obtain cultures allows bacteria to establish biofilm, which dramatically increases infection risk. Empirical antibiotics (cephalosporin ± aminoglycoside based on grade) must begin within 1 hour; cultures can be taken at debridement.

overallFeedback.feedback: Antibiotics must be given within 1 hour of presentation. This replaces the older 6-hour debridement rule. Bacteria start adhering to tissue within minutes, and within hours they form a biofilm that shields them from antibiotics and the immune system — early antibiotics prevent this, which no amount of later debridement can fully compensate for.
Exactly right. The 1-hour antibiotic window is the most time-critical intervention — it targets bacteria before they can form a protective biofilm on damaged tissue and hardware.

interactions.label: A 7-year-old with a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture cannot form

params.question: A 7-year-old with a displaced extension-type supracondylar fracture cannot form the OK sign (tip-to-tip pinch between thumb and index finger), but has completely normal sensation throughout the hand. Which nerve is most likely injured?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The radial nerve is more commonly injured in humeral shaft fractures, not supracondylar fractures. Its injury causes wrist drop and sensory loss over the dorsal first web space — neither is present here.

The ulnar nerve is more commonly injured in flexion-type supracondylar fractures. It causes weakness of intrinsic hand muscles and sensory loss over the little finger and ulnar half of the ring finger.

A complete median nerve injury would cause sensory loss over the thumb, index, middle, and radial half of the ring finger, in addition to motor weakness. Normal sensation here rules out a main trunk lesion.

The AIN is a pure motor branch of the median nerve, most commonly injured in extension-type supracondylar fractures. It supplies flexor pollicis longus and the index finger's flexor digitorum profundus — loss of these produces the characteristic inability to form the OK sign. Because it carries only motor fibres, sensation remains completely normal.

overallFeedback.feedback: The anterior interosseous nerve is the most commonly injured nerve in extension-type supracondylar fractures. It is a pure motor branch of the median nerve, so its injury abolishes the OK sign (FPL and index FDP paralysis) while keeping sensation completely normal — the critical distinction from a complete median nerve injury.
Correct. The AIN is a pure motor branch of the median nerve — the key distinguishing feature from a complete median nerve injury is that sensation is entirely preserved despite the motor deficit.
